title: Promote The Partner Who Already Runs Half The Company
excerptForBlog:
Ted Sarandos appointed co-CEO and elected to Board of Directors. Ted joined Netflix over 20 years ago, and we are thrilled to appoint him to be co-CEO with Reed. "Ted has been my partner for decades. This change makes formal what was already informal -- that Ted and I share the leadership of Netflix," says Hastings. Lead Independent director Jay Hoag says "Having watched Reed and Ted work together for so long, the board and I are confident this is the right step to evolve Netflix's management structure so that we can continue to best serve our members and shareholders for years to come." Ted will also continue to serve as Chief Content Officer. In addition, Greg Peters has been appointed COO adding to his Chief Product Officer role. "We want Greg to help us stay aligned and effective as we grow so quickly around the world," said Hastings.

In Q2, revenue grew 25% year over year, while quarterly operating income exceeded $1 billion. We added a Q2-record 10.1m paid memberships vs. 2.7m in last year's Q2. In the first half of this year, we've added 26m paid memberships, nearly on par with the 28m we achieved in all of 2019. However, growth is slowing as consumers get through the initial shock of Covid and social restrictions. We forecast 2.5m paid net adds for Q3'20 vs. 6.8m in the prior year quarter.

lessonTitle: Promote The Partner Who Already Runs Half The Company
lessonBody:
## 1. Core Message
Netflix made two structural changes during a blowout quarter. Ted Sarandos was named co-CEO alongside Reed Hastings and added to the board. Greg Peters was named COO on top of his Chief Product Officer role. The company did this while reporting 25% revenue growth, over $1 billion in quarterly operating income, and a record 10.1 million paid net adds — but also warning that growth was slowing fast, with Q3 forecast at just 2.5 million net adds versus 6.8 million the year before.

## 2. What the Executive Is Really Thinking
Hastings says the quiet part out loud: "This change makes formal what was already informal -- that Ted and I share the leadership of Netflix." The promotion isn't a new arrangement; it's a label catching up to reality. Doing it now, at a peak quarter, sends three signals at once: succession is handled, content leadership (Sarandos) sits at the same level as company leadership, and the operating layer (Peters as COO) is being reinforced before the next phase. The COVID surge gave Netflix cover to restructure from a position of strength rather than crisis. The forecast drop from 10.1m to 2.5m net adds tells you why management depth matters now — the easy growth is ending.

## 3. Key Management Lessons

### Make Titles Match Reality
#### What it means
If two people already share a job, give them both the title. Don't pretend one reports to the other when they don't.
#### Why it matters
Ambiguous power structures confuse employees, partners, and investors. They also create flight risk — talented operators leave when they feel under-titled.
#### MBA Perspective
This is Resource-Based View thinking. Sarandos's relationships with Hollywood and 20+ years of internal knowledge are a non-replicable asset. Locking him in with a co-CEO title and board seat protects that asset.
#### Real-world application
A founder with a co-founder running half the business should consider co-CEO or president titles early, instead of waiting for a competitor to offer the title first.

### Restructure From Strength, Not Weakness
#### What it means
Netflix announced leadership changes in the same letter as record results.
#### Why it matters
Big org changes during a bad quarter look like panic. The same changes during a great quarter look like planning.
#### MBA Perspective
No framework needed — this is timing and narrative control.
#### Real-world application
If you know a reorg is coming, pair it with a strong proof point. Earnings beat, big customer win, major launch. Same change, totally different reception.

### Separate the Content Engine From the Operating Engine
#### What it means
Sarandos keeps Chief Content Officer. Peters becomes COO on top of Chief Product Officer. The two halves of Netflix — what you watch and how you watch it — now have clear, elevated owners.
#### Why it matters
As a company scales globally, no single CEO can credibly run both creative and operations at depth. Splitting them lets each side move faster.
#### MBA Perspective
This is Vertical Integration management. Netflix owns content production and the distribution platform. Each layer now has a dedicated senior owner instead of one bottleneck.
#### Real-world application
A SaaS founder running both product and go-to-market past Series B usually needs to elevate one operator on each side. The job is two jobs.

### Announce Bad News Next to Good News
#### What it means
The letter celebrates the 10.1m net adds, then immediately warns Q3 will be 2.5m versus 6.8m a year earlier.
#### Why it matters
Investors punish surprises more than they punish bad numbers. Setting expectations during a victory lap is the cheapest time to do it.
#### MBA Perspective
No framework — just disciplined investor communication.
#### Real-world application
When you have a great month, that's the moment to flag the headwinds you see. Your credibility is highest, and the contrast cushions the warning.

## 4. Strategic Analysis (MBA Style)

### Competitive Strategy
Netflix is locking in its two most important non-Hastings executives at a moment when Disney+, HBO Max, and other streaming entrants are aggressively poaching talent. Title and board seat are retention tools.

### Risk Analysis
The document itself flags the main risk: "growth is slowing as consumers get through the initial shock of Covid." The leadership changes look designed to handle a harder operating environment where subscriber growth normalizes and execution — pricing, content efficiency, international rollout — starts to matter more than tailwinds.

### Build vs Buy Analysis
Not directly applicable. But note: Netflix is choosing to build leadership depth internally (promoting 20-year insiders) rather than hire a famous outside COO. The decision implicit here is build over buy on executive talent.

### Market Dynamics
Streaming is shifting from land-grab to operations. The fact that Netflix is naming a COO suggests the company sees the next chapter as operational scaling, not just growth.

### Long-Term Strategic Implications
If this works, Netflix has a clean succession plan and two strong second-tier leaders, reducing key-person risk on Hastings. If it fails, co-CEO structures historically create decision gridlock and unclear accountability — that's the real downside to watch.

## 5. Hidden Insights
- **Retention move disguised as a structure move.** Sarandos, with his Hollywood network, is one of the most poachable executives in media. Co-CEO and a board seat make leaving much more expensive.
- **The COO appointment hints at international complexity.** Hastings's quote — "help us stay aligned and effective as we grow so quickly around the world" — signals that global operations are now the hard problem.
- **The juxtaposition is the message.** Putting a leadership restructure in the same letter as a slowdown warning tells the market: we see what's coming, and we've already adjusted the org for it.
- **Succession is being normalized quietly.** Naming a co-CEO is the cleanest way to pre-stage a future CEO without making it a headline.
pullQuote: Formalizing power someone already has is cheaper than losing them — and clearer for everyone watching.
